Please let us know immediately if this proposal is acceptable to Plaintiff’s counsel, as your request for expedited oral argument on a portion of this proposal is pending before the Court with a response brief due tomorrow, and we intend to seek expedited relief on the issues related to Dr. Thundiyil’s research if we cannot reach agreement. Plaintiff’s failure to disclose required information related to Dr. Thundiyil’s publication related to highly relevant research and findings he relies upon in his expert report - Under FRCP 26, Dr. Thundiyil’s poster presentations should have been disclosed as both a publication and as “facts or data considered by the witness” when forming his opinion. See Thundiyil Depo. 16: 11–14 (first mention of the study looking at deaths in Florida); 17:10–20:10 (more details on the study); 105–108 (the “100 cases of kratom-related deaths” include the research he conducted, and more details on the studies). - Dr. Thundiyil’s CV was only current as April 2025 and Plaintiff’s expert disclosures were made in November 2025. Dr. Thundiyil acknowledged this should have been included on his CV. See Thundiyil Depo. 22:17– 21 (“A I see that, right. So I’m sorry, that is not the most recent. This version may not have it, but we can check, because sometimes I update the CV and forget to update the date.”); 24:1–2 (“Yeah, it does not look like it is on that draft of the CV.”). The fact that the poster presentations now appear on his current CV constitute a further acknowledgement that they should have been included as a publication. - The omitted news segments contain claims by Dr. Thundiyil that kratom is “compulsively addictive”; “interacts with different medications” and has “no proven medical benefits.” Additionally, in September 2025, Dr. Thundiyil publicly describes his “research” and “findings” explaining that a “group of us physicians essentially reached out to 25 medical examiners in the state of Floridia to try to answer the question are people dying from kratom” and we found some very interesting things” we “had medical examiners send us any reported deaths and found almost 40 deaths in state of FL over period of about 5 years.” Dr. Thundiyil claims “these are deaths in the absence of opioids, we know the chemical structure resembles opioids and that is what gave us this concern that it could cause death and we are still left with not knowing exactly why some people die and some don’t, but it still has some significant dangers with it.” See Thundiyil, Central Florida Doctor Unveils Kratom Research Findings, Potential Dangers. WESH 2 News on CW18, September 15, 2025. https://www.wesh.com/article/central-florida-doctor-unveils- kratom-research-findings-potential-dangers/66102687 1

Case 2:24-cv-00228-WBV-DPC Document 217-9 Filed 02/03/26 Page 3 of 12 - Dr. Thundiyil is representing to the public his “research” and “findings” on kratom related deaths, has relied on his study in his report and is now including these materials in his current CV after acknowledging that Plaintiff’s counsel did not provide the most updated version of his CV. Plaintiff had an obligation to list the omitted presentations and news segments in Dr. Thundiyil’s qualifications. See Shea v. Royal Enters., 2011 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 63763, at *21 (S.D.N.Y. June 16, 2011) (finding that the expert’s CV containing “select publications and presentations” was “not comprehensive with respect to his publications,” and ultimately excluded the expert). - Providing the CV in the middle of the deposition and providing limited materials after his deposition has concluded does not cure the prejudice Defendants incurred as a result of Plaintiff’s failure to comply with FRCP 26. Defendants did not have the opportunity to seek documents related to his research and presentation, provide materials related to his research and presentation to Defendants’ medical experts or adequately prepare for the deposition of Dr. Thundiyil. Other issues - As Dr. Huestis testified, some of the references she relied on in her report are publications based on the Nutrasource study. You have access to those publications. Johnson Foods will not produce the Nutrasource clinical study. This issue has been fully briefed before the Court, and the Court has declined to compel production of any documents related to the NDIN, which includes the Nutrasource study. See Dkt. 192. - With regards to Defendants’ supplemental production, such production was timely as it was produced well in advance of the fact discovery deadline. - However, the same cannot be said of Plaintiff’s recent production of Kathi Moller’s text messages, and the lack of any production from Jason Moller. Defendants’ RFPs beginning in November of 2024 have sought documents, including text messages, relating to Harmony Moller’s death and this lawsuit. Ms. Moller testified on December 14 that she never searched her phone for responsive messages, then one month later Plaintiff produced responsive text messages and improperly points to an off-the-record oral discussion between Plaintiff’s counsel and Maeghan Whitehead as an attempt to re-characterize Plaintiff’s deposition testimony. Moreover, the Subpoena issued to Jason Moller on November 17, 2025 included document requests for, inter alia, “All documents including but not limited to email, text messages, messages through any electronic, SMS, chats, or social media messaging platform, and other communications relating to Harmony Moller’s death on February 6, 2023 that relate to her cause of death or the events immediately preceding her death.” In response to this Subpoena, and in Jason’s deposition on December 17, 2025, he responded that he had no responsive documents. This is plainly false, as on January 16, 2025, Plaintiff produced a responsive text message between Jason and Kathi Moller which was not produced by Jason. Additionally, Plaintiff has produced one message in isolation without providing any reply or response so Plaintiff’s production is not complete. We propose that Plaintiff’s counsel and Defendants’ counsel continue to work through the discovery issues related to the parties through representations that can be made through counsel. There is no need to reopen party depositions based on documents that were produced within the fact discovery period. Additionally, as we move towards trial, we propose the parties work together to prioritize the issues that we must seek Court intervention on. Proposal related to experts Based on the above, we propose the following: 2

There is another issue that arose out of Friday’s deposition of Dr. Thundiyil that we need to resolve or understand whether we need to seek Court intervention so that these issues can be handled at the same time. Plaintiff’s expert disclosure on Nov. 18, 2025 for Dr. Thundiyil failed to comply with FRCP 26(a)(2)(B) as it did not include a “list of all publications authored in the previous 10 years.” Dr. Thundiyil’s CV was only current through 4/14/2025. His CV provided to Plaintiff on Friday during his deposition included multiple publications and presentations that are highly relevant to the issues in this case as they relate to studies involving mitragynine and causes of death (see below excerpts from Dr. Thundiyil’s updated CV). These publications all occurred before the Nov. 18 disclosure date. These studies came up during Dr. Thundiyil’s deposition. Defendants’ counsel repeatedly requested the materials and Dr. Thundiyil did not provide them. If these highly relevant materials had been disclosed, Defendant would have requested them in advance of Dr. Thundiyil’s deposition and been able to thoroughly question him on these topics. Defendant has been severely prejudiced by Plaintiff’s failure to comply with FRCP 26(a)(2)(B). As a result, Defendant requests that Plaintiff immediately provide all documents related to the below materials and that Plaintiff confirm that Dr. Thundiyil can be re-deposed on these topics. Please let us know if you agree or whether we need to raise this with the Court. Page 17: 5
